draft.title: Historical interpretations
card: An interpretation is a historian's explanation of the past, built from the evidence they have found. It is not the past itself. It is an account of what the evidence suggests happened.
Historians can read the same evidence in different ways. They may ask different questions, give some sources more weight, or fill gaps in the evidence with different ideas.
New evidence can change an interpretation. A newly found object, text or site may support an older explanation, or it may lead historians to revise it.
A good interpretation is based on evidence and can be explained with it. Comparing interpretations shows how historians reached their views.
draft.remember: An interpretation is an explanation built from evidence, and it can differ between historians or change with new evidence.

a.q: Two historians study the same ancient tomb paintings and explain them differently. What does this show about interpretations?
opts: Historians can interpret the same evidence differently
One of the two historians must have made up evidence
Interpretations are only opinions with no link to evidence
Evidence is useless if historians disagree about it
a.why: An interpretation is an explanation built from evidence, and historians may ask different questions or weigh sources differently. This can lead to different views. It does not mean either one invented evidence or that interpretations ignore evidence.
a.clue: Think about how each historian might use the same paintings.

b.q: Archaeologists in Egypt believed a town was built by a king for his priests. Then workers' tools, bakeries and homes were found there. Why might historians now revise their view?
opts: The new evidence may not fit the earlier explanation
The earlier explanation was not an interpretation at all
Historians always replace old views with new ones
The tools proved what the king had planned to do
b.why: New evidence can lead historians to revise an interpretation when it does not fit the earlier explanation. Here, the homes and bakeries suggest ordinary workers lived there. It is wrong to say historians always replace old views, because new evidence may also support them.
b.clue: Ask whether the new finds match the old explanation.

a.best: Historians can interpret the same evidence differently

b.best: The new evidence may not fit the earlier explanation
